target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would give workers the day off or more flexibility to vote
objection: A federal Election Day holiday would not reliably provide time off for many low-income retail and service workers, because federal law does not require private employers to give paid holidays and those workers would likely still be scheduled to work.

target: AG1’s claim that an Election Day holiday would significantly reduce scheduling barriers and increase turnout on its own
objection: Research indicates that having an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1’s preference for a holiday over other voting reforms
objection: Changing state laws to require employer time off for voting and/or implementing automatic voter registration are more reliable ways to improve voting access than making Election Day a federal holiday.

target: AG2’s objection that a holiday is not enough to improve turnout and is less targeted than other reforms
objection: Even if an Election Day holiday is not the only or most powerful turnout reform, it still has value because it changes voting into a civic celebration and thereby increases democratic participation.

target: AG2’s claim that other reforms make the holiday unnecessary
objection: An Election Day holiday still reduces scheduling barriers for many voters by giving them more time to vote, so it remains useful even if other reforms could also help.

target: AG2’s claim that school closures are not guaranteed by a federal holiday
objection: School-day obligations and weekday childcare constraints are real barriers to voting, and a federal holiday would likely free up daytime hours for parents and caregivers even if it does not affect every workplace.

target: AG1’s claim that school closures would reliably create a voting window for families
objection: Whether schools close is determined by local school districts and policies, not by the federal government’s holiday declaration, so a federal Election Day holiday would not reliably create that daytime window for parents and caregivers.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday would reliably help low-income families with childcare
objection: Low-income families often depend on predictable, low-cost school-based care; if schools do not close or if childcare must be arranged differently, the holiday may leave childcare constraints unchanged or make them more expensive.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reduce work-schedule barriers for many voters
objection: Because federal law does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, low-income retail and service workers would likely still have work conflicts with voting hours even on a federal holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday meaningfully addresses work-schedule barriers
objection: If a holiday does not reliably give time off to the workers most constrained by schedules, then it is not a dependable work-schedule voting-access reform.

target: AG1’s claim that Election Day’s holiday status would elevate civic participation more generally
objection: A holiday’s symbolic or perceptual benefits are unlikely to overcome the practical access problems that more direct voting-access reforms are designed to fix.

target: AG2’s claim that automatic voter registration is a better substitute for a holiday
objection: Automatic voter registration fixes registration barriers, but it does not remove the school and work schedule demands that still block many people from voting; the two reforms address different problems and do not replace each other.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would directly reduce school and work schedule barriers for many people
objection: Schools are not automatically closed by a federal holiday, and workplaces are not required to close or give paid leave, so the policy would not reliably reduce those scheduling barriers for the groups most constrained by them.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is justified even if it does not eliminate every scheduling barrier
objection: A policy should provide dependable voting-access improvements for the people most affected by schedule constraints; a federal holiday depends on third-party compliance and therefore does not reliably do that.

target: AG1’s claim that reducing some scheduling barriers is enough to justify the holiday
objection: If a holiday does not reliably remove the barriers that matter most for the most constrained voters, then it is not a dependable voting-access reform.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday lowers opportunity costs and therefore helps low-income workers
objection: For many low-income private-sector workers, a federal holiday would not guarantee paid time off and could still require unpaid time or lost wages to vote, so it may actually disadvantage them.

target: AG1’s claim that broad public support and international precedent make the holiday a good policy
objection: Bipartisan support and the fact that other countries hold elections on weekends or holidays do not, by themselves, show that the policy will actually improve voters’ ability to cast ballots.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday is reasonable because it is democracy-enhancing
objection: Policy adoption should depend on expected real-world effects on voting access, especially for people most constrained by work and school schedules, rather than on popularity or symbolic democratic framing.

target: AG1’s implication that the holiday would not disadvantage low-income workers
objection: Low-income retail and service workers are more likely to face private-employer schedules and high opportunity costs, so a federal Election Day holiday could preserve work-hour conflicts and disadvantage them.

target: AG2’s claim that holidays do not reliably create a school-day voting window
objection: School-day constraints and weekday childcare/daytime timing are real barriers to voting, so closing schools or easing school obligations would still help many families and caregivers even if not every school district follows the same schedule.
